name: Lena Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the filler and capper on Line 3 at a soft-drinks bottling plant, out by the ring road. I clock in at six, check the nozzles, load the cap hopper, and then spend most of the shift listening for the sound that means a bottle's jammed in the star wheel. I'm still slow at changeovers, honestly. Marek, who trained me, can switch from the half-litre to the two-litre in twenty minutes and it takes me nearly forty.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real. At the end of the day there are pallets of something people actually drink, and I can point at them. What wears me out is the noise and the standing, and the new screens they keep adding to the line that I have to learn all over again. I'm not a screen person, I still pay my bills at the post office counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Everyone at the plant was scared of the robots taking over and it turned into a few new screens and some emails from head office. I'd probably say it on the union group chat, that's about as online as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it'd be a relief. It means I can keep getting better at the line without feeling like I'm learning a job that's about to vanish. I'd still want the union to watch what the bosses do with the time they save, because saved time has a way of turning into fewer people on a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep putting money aside like I do now, a bit over a third of my pay, and I'd ask Marek to keep teaching me the changeovers until I can do one under thirty minutes. Maybe I'd finally pay the plumber to fix the boiler in the flat my sister and I own, instead of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a fire alarm that turned out to be someone's toast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said saved time turns into fewer people on a shift. Have you seen that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, two years ago, before I started properly. They put an automatic case packer on Line 1 and the shift went from five people to three. Nobody was sacked, they just didn't replace two women who retired, and that's how it always goes, quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marek about all this, over lunch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, see, we're still here, now show me the trick with the guide rails again. He'd laugh and say something about how they said the same thing about the internet. We eat in the van mostly, because the canteen is too loud.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so: everyone feared robots and it turned into a few new screens and emails from head office. I'd post it on the union group chat, which is about as online as I get.
S0.think: It's a relief, because I can keep getting better at the line without fearing it'll vanish. I'd still want the union watching what bosses do with saved time, because that time quietly turns into fewer people per shift.
S0.do: Keeps saving over a third of her pay and asks Marek to keep training her until she can do a changeover in under thirty minutes. Pays for the overdue boiler repair in the flat she co-owns with her sister.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, with a small background watchfulness about headcount.
S0.quote: Nobody was sacked, they just didn't replace two women who retired, and that's how it always goes, quietly.
S0.fieldNote: Even in the calmest picture, her mind goes straight to headcount and the union. She's openly behind on skill and says so without embarrassment. Her distance from technology is part of her identity: she still pays bills at the post office counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need a strong union and proper rules. If the company gets a robot that does half my job, the workers should share in that, through shorter hours or retraining paid by them, not by us. I'd say it loudly at the branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the one they'd move first. I'm junior and I'm slow, and I don't want to learn some new computer system every six months. The good news is there are four other bottling and canning plants within half an hour, so if it gets bad here I could probably walk into one of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting instead of every other one, and I'd push for a written deal on retraining before any new machine goes in. I'd keep my savings where they are and not touch them. If they offered me a course on the new system, I'd take it, but only because the alternative is being pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like the ground's a bit soft, not falling in, but I'd feel it with every step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take a course only because the alternative is being pushed out. What makes new systems so hard for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not that I'm stupid, it's that I learn with my hands and my ears. I know Line 3 by the sound it makes, and a screen doesn't make a sound until it beeps at you that something's wrong. Every time they update the software the menus move, and I feel like a beginner again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the plant asked for volunteers to move to a different line or a new role, would you put your hand up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd wait to be asked. I know that's not the clever answer. But I've only just stopped being the new girl on Line 3, and I don't want to start again somewhere else while everybody watches.

S1.say: I'd say this is why we need a strong union and proper rules, so workers share in what robots save through shorter hours or company-paid retraining. I'd say it loudly at the branch meeting.
S1.think: Privately she knows she'd be moved first because she's junior and slow and doesn't want new systems every six months. She takes comfort that four other bottling and canning plants are within half an hour.
S1.do: Attends every union meeting and pushes for a written retraining deal before any new machine arrives. Leaves her savings untouched and accepts a course on new systems only if pushed, not by choice.
S1.feel: Uneasy, as if the ground has gone soft, though nothing is falling in yet.
S1.quote: I know Line 3 by the sound it makes, and a screen doesn't make a sound until it beeps at you that something's wrong.
S1.fieldNote: There's a clear gap between her loud public line about workers sharing gains and her private wish to just be left alone on her line. Her plenty-of-jobs backstop keeps her from real fear. She learns by sound and touch, which explains much of her dislike of screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster, and that governments let a handful of tech companies do this to everyone without asking. I'd be on the march, whatever march there was. I'd want robot owners taxed hard and the money paid out to people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. My whole plan was to get good at this, maybe become a line lead by thirty, and that plan would just be gone. The other plants nearby won't help me either, because they'd all be buying the same robots at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent or food, and I'd talk to my sister about whether we rent out our grandmother's flat for income or sell it before prices drop. I'd join whatever action the union organised, strikes included. I wouldn't try to learn AI, I'd be too angry and I wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be doing sums at night. What are the numbers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got about eight months of my normal spending saved, and my half of the flat. If I cut back to just the basics, maybe a year and a bit. Nadia's a nurse, so in theory her job lasts longer, but if robots can do hands-on work, I don't know that it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you wouldn't touch AI even then. Is there a version where you'd change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the union ran a course and I sat in a room with people I know, maybe. I don't trust learning it alone from a phone. But if it's going to do every job anyway, what am I learning it for, to train my own replacement?

S2.say: I'd say it's a disaster and governments let a few tech companies do this to everyone without asking. I'd be on any march going, demanding robot owners be taxed hard and the money paid out to workers.
S2.think: Two years wipes out her plan to become a line lead by thirty. She's sure nearby plants won't save her, because they'd all be buying the same robots at the same time.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent and food and talks with her sister about renting out or selling their inherited flat. Joins any union action including strikes, but refuses to learn AI because she's angry and unsure where to start.
S2.feel: Alarmed and angry, lying awake doing sums about how long her money lasts.
S2.quote: But if it's going to do every job anyway, what am I learning it for, to train my own replacement?
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario breaks her one comfort, the nearby plants, and that's what tips her from uneasy to alarmed. Her savings buy time but she doesn't see what the time is for. She'd only learn new tech in a room with people she knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan. I'd want laws in place by then, a robot tax, a guaranteed income, something. I'd say it at work and I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd be thirty-two when it lands. It's better than two, because I could save a lot more and watch what happens to the first plants that automate. But it's the same cliff, I'd just see it from further away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder for the first few years, maybe half my pay, and I'd get onto the union's regional committee so I'm in the room when deals get made. My sister and I would probably keep the flat and rent it out, because a roof is worth more than cash if everything goes strange. I'd keep my job right up to the end, I'm not leaving early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more the kind where you're busy than the kind where you can't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said nearby plants wouldn't save you. With five years, would they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while maybe. The first plant to go full robot would be the big canning one, they've got the money. The small family bottler on the other side of town would be last, so I might hop there for a couple of years. But that's buying time, not a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your job right up to the end. Why not get out ahead of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because where would I go that's safe? If every job goes, leaving early just means I lose my pay sooner. And I'd want to be inside the plant, on the shop floor, when the union's fighting about how it ends.

S3.say: I'd say with five years there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan, a robot tax or a guaranteed income. I'd say it at work and sign every petition going.
S3.think: Five years is better than two because she can save more and watch the first plants automate. But she sees it as the same cliff, just seen from further away.
S3.do: Saves up to half her pay and joins the union's regional committee. Keeps and rents out the flat with her sister, considers hopping to a small family bottler for a couple of years, and stays on the shop floor to the end.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, with energy to act rather than freeze.
S3.quote: But it's the same cliff, I'd just see it from further away.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn fear into organising. She uses time to save and to get into the room where deals are made, not to retrain. Her logic for staying is sharp: leaving early just means losing pay sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so let's do it properly. Shorter weeks, a share of the profits for workers, public money for whatever comes next. If they mess it up with ten years' warning, that's a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven. That's a lot of years of normal life before it hits, and I'd probably be a decent operator by then, maybe even a line lead. Then it all goes anyway, and I'd have spent my best years getting good at something nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on like now for the first few years, saving and learning the line, because I don't trust predictions that far out. Around year five I'd start a proper evening course in something with people in it, like care work or teaching kids, if those still look like they need humans. I'd keep pushing the union and vote for whoever promised a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slow way. Like knowing about a dentist appointment months away that you can't cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care work or teaching. Why those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Nadia comes home from the ward with stories that no robot could have handled, the old man who only eats if you sit with him. I'm not sure a robot can't do it, but I'm sure people would want it from a person. Nobody's ever wanted a bottle capped by a person, have they?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait five years before starting. Isn't that cutting it close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've seen the plant announce three big changes since I started and two never happened. I'd rather move once, when I'm sure, than chase every rumour and end up good at nothing.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly: shorter weeks, a profit share for workers and public money for what comes next. If they mess it up with that much warning, it's a choice.
S4.think: She'd be thirty-seven and finally good at the job just as it disappears. She fears spending her best years mastering something nobody needs.
S4.do: Carries on saving and learning the line for about five years, then starts an evening course in care work or teaching children if those still need people. Keeps pushing the union and votes for a real plan.
S4.feel: A slow, steady anxiety, like an appointment months away that she can't cancel.
S4.quote: Nobody's ever wanted a bottle capped by a person, have they?
S4.fieldNote: More time doesn't make her calmer, it just pushes the worry into the future and adds the sting of wasted effort. Her partner's nursing stories shape where she'd go next. Her resistance shows as waiting until she's sure, which she defends with real past examples.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. With ten years I can be angry and organised, with two I'd just be angry. What would help is the union having a deal ready before it happens, and the government guaranteeing an income while people like me find our feet, not a means-tested form that takes six months.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. Everyone asks what I'd do, but nobody asks who owns the robots that do my job. If it was the workers or the town, I'd feel completely different about all five pictures.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks what I'd do, but nobody asks who owns the robots that do my job.
portrait: Lena Ito is a 27-year-old junior operator on the filler and capper line of a soft-drinks bottling plant, still slower at changeovers than the man who trained her. She has about eight months of spending saved and co-owns a flat with her sister, and her partner Nadia is a nurse. A committed union member who learns by sound and touch, she dislikes screens and never uses AI. She stays calm if AI stalls, turns to organising as change speeds up, and becomes alarmed only when AGI arrives in two years and her backstop of nearby plants disappears.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because with two years she'd only have time to be angry, not organised.
whatWouldHelp: A union deal agreed before the change arrives, and a guaranteed income from the government while people find their feet, without a slow means-tested process.
